opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those ideas that comes up every couple of years, and I understand the intuition behind it. The story goes something like: adversarial examples exist because these models are hugely overparameterized, so there's all this slack, all these unused directions in the network that an attacker can exploit. If you squeeze the model down, prune it, quantize it, distill it, then maybe you remove that slack and the attacks have nowhere to go.

It's a nice story. I just don't think it's true, and the evidence we have mostly points the other way.

First, empirically, small models are not more robust. If you take a tiny network, even a linear classifier, you can still find adversarial examples. The original explanations for adversarial examples, things like the linearity hypothesis, basically say that in high-dimensional input spaces, lots of tiny perturbations across many input dimensions add up to a big change in the output. That's a property of the input dimensionality and the geometry of the decision boundary. It isn't a property of having too many parameters. So shrinking the model doesn't touch the actual cause.

Second, there's a long history of defenses that look like they work because of compression, and then fall apart. Quantization is the classic case. If you quantize activations or inputs, gradients become zero almost everywhere, so a naive gradient-based attack stops working and the defense looks great. But you haven't made the model robust. You've made it hard to compute gradients. That's gradient masking, or obfuscated gradients. Once you use something like a straight-through estimator, or just approximate the non-differentiable piece with a smooth one, the attack works again, often at almost the same perturbation size. A lot of the defenses we broke a few years ago fall into exactly that category.

Third, if anything there's a decent argument that robustness needs more capacity, not less. Some of the adversarial training work found that bigger models get more benefit from adversarial training. Intuitively, a robust classifier has to learn a more complicated decision boundary, one that stays correct across a whole ball around each training point instead of just at the points. That's a harder function to represent, so you'd expect it to need more parameters. Compressing a model may actually be removing capacity you'd want for robustness.

So my general view is that compression is useful for lots of reasons, like efficiency, deployment, and cost, but it isn't a security mechanism. And the meta-lesson, the thing I keep saying, is that whenever someone proposes a defense, the question isn't whether the attacks you tried failed. It's whether you tried an adaptive attack that knows about the defense and is designed to get around it. Compression-based defenses almost always look good against non-adaptive attacks and much less good against adaptive ones.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unused directions as part of the compression hypothesis, but does not distinguish unused weights from unused directions in activation space.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says small models are not more robust and that compression is not a security mechanism.

r003.rationale: It discusses high-dimensional perturbations and decision-boundary geometry, but not attacks activating classification features atypically for a particular input.

r004.rationale: The response does not say compression preserves exploitable features because those features are needed for classification.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest adversarial training reduces ordinary-data accuracy by suppressing classification features.

r006.rationale: It says compression does not remove the underlying cause of attacks, but does not connect incomplete robustness from adversarial training to directions that cannot all be removed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is an idea that comes up over and over again, and I understand why it's intuitively appealing. The story goes something like: adversarial examples exist because the network has all this excess capacity, all these extra degrees of freedom that it isn't using for the actual task, and the attacker exploits that slack. So if you compress the model, prune it, quantize it, distill it down, you squeeze out the slack and there's nowhere left for the adversary to hide. It's a nice story. It's just not what happens.

The first thing I'd say is that we've seen essentially this argument, in different clothing, many times. Defensive distillation back in 2015 was more or less this. Various quantization-as-defense papers made the same claim. And every time, when you actually sit down and evaluate properly, the robustness disappears. Usually what happened is that the compression changed the gradients in some way, made them noisier, or flatter, or quantized them, and the standard attack that was run in the paper stopped working. But that's gradient masking, not robustness. If you take a step back and run a stronger attack, or a black-box attack, or just transfer adversarial examples from the uncompressed model, they go right through. So I'd be very cautious about any result here that doesn't come with an adaptive evaluation.

The second thing, and I think this is the deeper point, is that the premise is wrong about where adversarial examples come from. They're not really a bug in the extra parameters. One of the things Ilyas and others showed a few years ago is that adversarial perturbations are largely features. They're directions in input space that are genuinely predictive of the label on the training distribution, they're just imperceptible to us. A compressed model that still gets good accuracy still has to use those features, because they're useful. So compression doesn't remove the vulnerability, it just packs it into fewer weights. If anything, you'd expect a smaller model to have less capacity to learn the robust, human-aligned features, which are harder to learn, and that's roughly what the empirical results say. Adversarially trained models tend to want to be bigger, not smaller.

And then there's a practical point. Even if there were some capacity argument to be made, the attacker only needs a few directions. A model with ten parameters that's doing linear classification in high dimensions is already vulnerable, that's the original Goodfellow argument. The attack doesn't need a huge hypothesis class to exploit, it needs an input space with lots of dimensions, and compressing the model doesn't change the input space at all.

So where I land is: compression is a great thing to do for efficiency, and it mostly leaves robustness about where it was, sometimes slightly worse. If someone shows you a compressed model that looks robust, the first question should be whether the attack was actually adapted to the defense, and the second should be whether adversarial examples from the original model still transfer. In my experience the answer to the second one is almost always yes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unused capacity and high-dimensional input space, but does not distinguish unused weights from unused directions in activation space.

r002.rationale: It says compression does not remove the vulnerability and that robustness mostly stays the same or can get slightly worse.

r003.rationale: It describes adversarial perturbations as predictive, imperceptible features, but does not say they activate features in ways atypical of the particular input.

r004.rationale: It explains that an accurate compressed model still needs useful predictive features, so compression preserves those exploitable features.

r005.rationale: It says robust features are harder to learn and adversarially trained models tend to need more capacity, but does not connect adversarial training to lower ordinary-data accuracy from suppressing classification features.

r006.rationale: It argues that a few directions in high-dimensional input space can enable attacks, but does not say adversarial training fails because it cannot remove all adversarial directions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting hypothesis, but I don’t think compression by itself gives you a reason to expect adversarial examples to disappear. Making a model smaller and making it robust are different objectives. You can have a very small model with a decision boundary that’s very close to some of its inputs, and that’s enough to allow adversarial examples.

The intuition, I think, is that a large network has all this extra capacity, and maybe attacks exploit something stored in that excess capacity. But an attack doesn’t necessarily need the network to have memorized some unusual behavior. It can exploit the same features the network uses to make its ordinary predictions. If compression preserves those features, it may preserve the vulnerability too.

So I’d want to test it. Compress the model, then construct attacks specifically against the compressed model. If attacks against the original model stop working, that’s interesting, but it doesn’t establish that the compressed model is robust. It may just mean you need a different attack.

r001.rationale: The response discusses model size and decision boundaries but does not distinguish unused weights from unused directions in activation space.

r002.rationale: It says compression alone gives no reason to expect adversarial examples to disappear and that small models can still be vulnerable.

r003.rationale: It says attacks may exploit features used for ordinary predictions, but does not state that they activate those features in ways atypical of the particular input.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says compression may preserve the features used for ordinary predictions, and thus preserve vulnerability.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss adversarial training or its effect on accuracy.

r006.rationale: The response does not discuss adversarial training or whether some adversarial directions cannot be removed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an intuition there, but I don’t think compression by itself gives you that guarantee. The intuition is that if a network has a lot of excess capacity, maybe some of that capacity is being used to represent these strange behaviors, and if we remove it, those behaviors go away.

But an adversarial example isn’t necessarily something the network has memorized or set aside space for. It can be a consequence of the decision boundary that the network learned. Even a very simple linear classifier can have adversarial examples. So you don’t need a large, complicated network for this problem to exist.

Compression could change robustness, and it might improve it in some cases. But the question is whether the compressed model actually becomes more robust when you attack it directly. If you take attacks generated against the original model and find that they no longer work after compression, that doesn’t establish that the vulnerabilities are gone. You have to let the attacker adapt to the compressed model.

r002.rationale: It says compression alone gives no guarantee and may improve robustness in some cases; it does not state that compression does not make networks more robust.

r003.rationale: It does not describe adversarial attacks as activating classification-useful features atypically for a particular input.

r004.rationale: It attributes adversarial examples to learned decision boundaries but does not say compression preserves exploitable features because they are needed for classification.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss adversarial training or a possible accuracy cost on ordinary data.
